title: Vox Media Should Be Ashamed of This Headline
description: I saw a headline this week that made me genuinely angry, and I don’t say that lightly. It was one of those big, hopeful, a-corner-has-been-turned Alzheimer’s headlines. The kind that a woman whose mother is slipping away reads on her phone at midnight and feels her chest unclench for a second. The kind that makes a family think, maybe. Maybe there’s something now. So I paid the two dollars and I read the whole thing. And here’s the strange part. The article itself is more careful than the headline. The reporter quotes the risks. He even notes that hype has outpaced the science before. But almost nobody reads the whole article. They read the headline, they feel the glow of it, and they walk away believing we are closer to a cure than we are. That gap, between what a skimmed headline implies and what the science actually says, is the thing that hurts real people. So let me walk you through what the science actually says. The story is really about two drugs. Lecanemab and donanemab. You may have seen the brand names, Leqembi and Kisunla. They are, to be fair, real progress, and I won’t take that from them. They are the first drugs that have clearly, definitively slowed the cognitive decline of Alzheimer’s in large trials. For a disease that has humiliated every treatment thrown at it for decades, that matters. But here is what the headline does not tell you, and what every family deserves to know before their hope gets hijacked. These drugs do not make anyone better. Let me be precise, because precision is the whole point here. In the trials, lecanemab slowed decline by about 27% and donanemab by around 35% over eighteen months (van Dyck et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2023; Sims et al., JAMA, 2023).

title: Are you happier if you get more sunlight?
description: Team, A morning-light study caught my attention because of what improved—and what didn’t. Thirty-three university students felt less sleepy after a week of morning bright-light exposure. But their performance on attention and memory tests didn’t improve. That is an interesting result if, like me, you spend your working life asking what actually helps the brain. First, what did the study actually show? In the July 2026 preprint, participants completed one week using a 10,000-lux light device for 30 minutes each morning and another week under their usual lighting conditions. The order was randomized. During the bright-light week, they reported less daytime sleepiness, with the largest difference at midday. The researchers also reported improved Fitbit-estimated sleep efficiency and more consistent sleep duration. But the cognitive tests did not show improvement. This was a small, short study with no washout period between conditions, and it has not been certified by peer review. It cannot settle whether morning light improves cognition more broadly. It also tested a device, not a few minutes outdoors. My interpretation: encouraging findings for sleepiness and sleep patterns, without a demonstrated memory benefit in this experiment. I would happily take a less sleepy afternoon. I would just like us to describe it accurately. Why would light affect your brain in the first place? Your retina does more than help you see. It contains intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells , or ipRGCs. These cells detect light through a pigment called melanopsin , while also receiving input originating from rods and cones. Some send signals directly to the suprachiasmatic nucleus , or SCN, in the hypothalamus: your central circadian clock.

title: You have health insurance. Why are you still fighting for care?
description: Team, A woman with breast cancer is under anesthesia. Her mastectomy has already begun. In another operating room, her reconstructive surgeon, Dr. Elisabeth Potter, is finishing a case when a nurse comes in with an unusual message: UnitedHealthcare is on the phone, and they need to speak to her right now . The call is about the woman currently undergoing surgery. The insurance company wants Potter to explain the patient’s diagnosis and justify why she needs to remain in the hospital overnight. The patient has breast cancer. She is already unconscious. Her surgery was authorized. Her physicians have determined the care she needs. And yet, in the middle of the operation, her surgeon is being asked to step away and defend it. Potter told me that in that moment she felt like she was having to “protect my patient from her insurance company.” The overnight stay was ultimately denied anyway, and the patient received a bill for $100,000 . After Potter spoke publicly about what happened and the story exploded online, she says the bill was erased. But that immediately raises a much more disturbing question: what happens to the patient whose doctor doesn’t have a viral video? Your nervous system needs inputs, too Taking an active role in your health also means paying attention to the stress you carry every day—and making room for recovery before you’re completely depleted. Between work, training, travel and caring for the people around you, “just relax” can feel like one more thing on an already unreasonable to-do list. That’s one of the reasons I’ve been using Nuropod .
